title: Weekly Trading Desk Talk: Burnin’ Up
summary: Inflation is heating up again, but the longer-term picture remains more measured.
body_markdown:
***Burnin’ Up***


Last week’s release of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) report for October showed that costs for goods and services rose more than expected last month across several sectors, providing new warning signs to the Federal Reserve in its fight against inflation. When reading the data and subsequent Fedspeak, the lyrics from the 2008 Jonas Brothers’ hit come to mind: “I’m slippin’ into the lava, and I’m tryin’ to keep from goin’ under … baby who turned the temperature hotter? ‘Cause I’m burnin’ up, burnin’ up.”


October’s CPI report is one of the last reports that the Fed will see before next month’s meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Given the Fed’s heightened focus on inflation, a December rate hike now appears all but certain.


Returning to the latest inflation data, CPI rose by 0.4% in October; stripping out volatile food and energy costs, core CPI also increased more than forecasted, rising 0.3% month over month. (The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish year-over-year data thanks to last fall’s government shutdown which disrupted data collection.) Looking at individual sectors, energy rose 0.7% last month, mainly driven by a 1% increase in gasoline prices and a 0.9% jump in electricity. Food inflation was also robust: Meat, dairy, and vegetables all saw strong increases, while cereals and nonalcoholic beverages saw price decreases.


While the latest CPI report points to renewed inflation momentum and strengthens the case for additional monetary policy tightening, the longer-run trend remains considerably more benign (Figure 1). That’s because the recent pickup in inflation appears to be concentrated in short-term measures caused by higher energy prices and persistent service-sector inflation, while the six- and 12-month annualized rates continue to indicate that underlying inflation pressures are gradually cooling, rather than reaccelerating broadly across the economy.


Escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have contributed significantly to upward pressure on energy markets in recent months. Although energy prices are excluded from core inflation measures, sustained increases in energy prices can indirectly affect transportation, travel, and other service-sector costs, creating a potential headwind for disinflation.


Meanwhile, headline CPI (the white line in Figure 2) moderated significantly from September. However, the composition of October’s report is arguably more meaningful than the headline slowdown; a smaller contribution from energy helped reduce overall inflation, but core services remained elevated and continued to account for most of the monthly price pressures. Because the Fed tends to consider core inflation as a measure of underlying price trends, the report is unlikely to alter policymakers’ view that inflation is cooling.


Core services exclude food and energy and include categories like rent, medical services, education, auto insurance, and transportation. The Fed monitors core services especially closely because service-sector inflation is closely tied to wage growth, labor market shortages, and domestic demand. Unlike goods prices, which can fall quickly when supply chains improve or inventories build up, prices for services tend to be much stickier. In October, rent for primary residences rose 0.2%, while travel lodging prices increased 0.6% and airfares were up 0.4%.


Though headline CPI decelerated from September, nearly 60% of October’s inflation came from core services. This is significant because service-sector inflation tends to be driven by wage growth and domestic demand, making it more difficult for the Fed to bring inflation back to target through supply-side improvements alone.


The CPI report also arrived at an important inflection point for the Fed as it prepares for December’s meeting and interest-rate decision. Ahead of the release last Tuesday morning, Fed Governor Christopher Waller delivered notably hawkish remarks in London: If CPI came in hot, Waller said that “a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.” Waller went on to define hot inflation as a core CPI monthly increase of “around 0.3%.”


Just a few hours later, core CPI did, indeed, come in at exactly 0.3%, leading traders to begin placing bets on a Fed rate hike next month. As it stands, a quarter-point hike is now fully priced in, with more hawkish traders hedging for the possibility of a half-point hike at a 14% probability. Several other Fed officials spoke last week and followed Waller’s lead. For example, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan spoke on Tuesday and said that she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases: “It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall. After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate.” Likewise, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Tuesday that “inflation pressures are still very much with us. For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate, but the exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I’ll be watching the data closely.”


New York Fed President John Williams, a historically dovish voter, nevertheless added to the hawkish tone on Thursday: “Inflation is far too high and it continues to be high even in the latest data. We’ll need to take actions over time that will ensure we get back to our 2% goal promptly and on a sustained basis.” Williams was less explicit than Waller or Logan regarding the magnitude of future rate hikes, yet his remarks reinforced the growing consensus within the Fed and the market that additional tightening is warranted.


In short, last week’s data reinforces the notion that the final phase of the inflation fight may prove the most difficult. Longer-term inflation trends continue to point toward gradual disinflation, but October’s report still demonstrated that progress remains uneven and heavily influenced by persistent service-sector price pressures. Fed officials appear increasingly prepared to keep monetary policy restrictive for longer and remain open to additional tightening—should inflation continue burnin’ up.


FROM THE DESK
**Agency CMBS —** Last week was slightly disjointed, given the mid-week holiday. Fannie Mae spreads were one basis point (bp) tighter on Monday and remained flat the rest of the week. Fannie Mae DUS volume picked up last week to roughly $910 million, up 66% from the previous week and 54% above the trailing four-week average. The uptick in volume was anchored by two large block trades ($509 million and $159 million), which made up about 74% of the total. Ginnie Mae volume, on the other hand, was lighter last week. About $200 million came to market, down from about $900 million a week earlier. Ginnie spreads were three bps wider week over week.


**Municipals —** AAA tax-exempt yields moved higher across the curve last week, reversing a month-long trend of declining rates. Yields rose by as much as 17 bps on the front end of the curve, even though issuance remained light; less than $10 billion in new supply came to market. We expect issuance to pick up next week before activity slows heading into Thanksgiving. Short-term, cash-collateralized structures also experienced some spread widening during the week. Fund flows turned negative following five consecutive weeks of inflows, with municipal funds posting $176 million of outflows. High-yield funds were responsible for about 64% of the outflows.
